item.title: Devbhoomi Indeed
item.dc:creator: divyaprakashpoddar
item.content:encoded: It was late night and we had climbed all the way to the top making our way through narrow paths lit up by the torch-light of our phones. For a few of us the vision would blur at regular intervals, which indicated it was time to stop and clean up our glass lenses from the raindrops and perspiration. So anyway, we got to the top, and then to reach Deoria Tal, we started going down a slope. The thick forest suddenly ended on our right and we saw a huge meadow illuminated by the moonlight. There were a few tents and at one end there was the Taal which we were so eager to reach. From our height, the Taal did not seem all that awe-inspiring. (We realized later that we were deceived of its scale. In the mountains, you are never sure what the actual size of things are, until you get very close.) After surveying the meadow and the Taal for a while, we moved our eyes to the sky and I became Spellbound, but gradually. It seemed that a humongous cloud was lying over the horizon, which made sense since it had been raining a few moments earlier. However, there was something about those clouds I couldn't quite put my finger on. Wind blew, and some part of the cloud moved away and only then did I realize that the Huge cloud we had been staring at was not after all a cumulonimbus, but it was the mighty Chaukhambha. We knew we would get to see it once we reached the top, but we never expected it to be this gigantic. I had seen photos before and you would be seeing them too in my post, but these photos fail miserably to convey the size of these mountains. You have to be here to feel like an insignificant being while in their surroundings. The Gibbous moon although bright, wasn't enough for our human eyes to admire the Massif in front of us in complete detail. I had got my camera along with the tripod and I had hoped to attempt Night time landscape photography for the first time. I hadn't known much about DSLR photography even though I owned one. (It was one of those things you buy while in an engineering college in India). So I set up the tripod and camera, tried to manually focus on the mountains, and let the auto mode take care of the rest. The shutter remained open for about 3-4 seconds and I waited for the result. Heavenly! How else would someone describe it? We associate the heavens with the unattainable and mystical and these were exactly the emotions that the image welled up in my mind. (I have a theory for why these mountains feel so heavenly, but that is for another post.) Somehow after clicking that picture I was able to admire the mountains even more clearly with my eyes. There are some emotions inside of you which get activated when you are in a certain surrounding and this definitely was such a place. Its not possible to describe them using human language and I will not  attempt it. But during that night I felt the closest to the heavens and I am sure all my companions did too. Its not enough to hear from someone that Uttarakhand is Devbhoomi. You've got to feel it yourself and believe me, you will! [caption id="attachment_23" align="alignnone" width="4898"] A testament to my skills in using a DSLR at night[/caption]

item.title: Morning at Rudranath
item.dc:creator: divyaprakashpoddar
item.content:encoded:
Having finally caught some sleep after shivering from the bone chilling cold most of the night, I started dreaming of the incredible vistas I had seen during the day. In dreams, one's subconscious usually comes up with images which are fantasy but obviously my brain had difficulty conjuring up images any better than the one it had already seen the previous day. Thus all I could see in my dreams were the beautiful pathways I had trodden all day. These images seemed as unbelievable as they did during the day as they did in my sleep.

The dream ended and I woke up happily, completely aware of the fact that apart from my eyes being open now, nothing else has changed. I got out of the layers of (Heavy) blankets and opened the door of our stone house which had kept the insides relatively warm. Stepping outside in the cold morning, the sight in front of me stirred a primal fear within. The sight of sharp and tall, humongous mountains forming an inescapable wall on the horizon intimidated me. Being afraid was the last feeling I had expected to encounter in such a divine place. I felt imprisoned.

However fear turned into astonishment as my brain started processing the shapes of each of these peaks. I realized that I was being offered views of all the mountain peaks which had eluded me the earlier day. There it was the mighty Nanda Devi, the second tallest peak in India and then Brahmkamal and also Dronagiri and wait there was Trishul too! All presenting their silhouettes with the sun rising behind them. I had been in Uttarakhand for almost a year (and been to Auli thrice!) but hadn't been deemed worthy of a glimpse of Nanda Devi peak. However climbing all the way to Rudranath must have convinced the weather gods to bestow upon me this wonderful view!

[caption id="attachment_34" align="alignnone" width="4898"] Nanda Devi Peak (7816 meters) Wikipedia[/caption] [caption id="attachment_32" align="alignnone" width="4898"] Brahmakamal[/caption] [caption id="attachment_33" align="alignnone" width="4898"] Dronagiri/Dunagiri Peak (7066 meters) Wikipedia[/caption] I got my camera out and clicked away. Gathering materials for more stories which I plant to narrate in the future. As a bonus I also got to see Nanda Devi on my fourth visit to Auli! [caption id="attachment_37" align="alignnone" width="4898"] Nanda Devi Peak as visible from Auli[/caption]

item.title: Samosas in Bangalore
item.dc:creator: divyaprakashpoddar
item.content:encoded:
The faint aroma of samosas being fried was making me impatient. It takes forever for the Samosa to reach the magical golden brown. The halwai seems to tease you with his ladle motions and Just when it seems that he is going take the bunch out of the humongous kadhai, he puts them back in.

I was ready to wait.

Finally I was served a plate of crisp, hot samosas. I picked them up with reverence and proceeded to perform the chutney dipping ritual. However, I wasn't ready for the sacrilege laid out on the plate. The place of Imley chutney was taken by a white paste. Outraged, I inquired the halwai about this unholy act. He glared at me and mumbled something in a language I didn't understand. He then casually took a bottle of parachute coconut hair oil and poured it completely into the kadhai, while I watched in utter horror and started shaking uncontrollably in disbelief.

"Wake up, we are about to reach Chennai", said my mother while shaking me to wake me up. Oh what a nightmare it was, having to see my most favorite dish treated in such a way probably scarred my mind and my appetite for the rest of my life.

The train stopped at a platform and vendors went up and down the aisle introducing their wares in the most unusual way like always. I wondered if someone actually sold something announcing the name in a normal way, he would definitely be ignored.

Anyway I was listening to each one of them with concentration, trying to decipher the words so as to decide, if they actually were of any interest to me.

"Chaaaiii....", No!, "Paaeeper....", Boring!, "Vadae....," I Wonder what that is? This went on for a few minutes and it seemed that none would receive my business or my father's to be precise.

"Saaamosees…", the magical words were uttered at last although heavily distorted. These words cast a spell on me and caused me to throw my hands excitedly, stomp my foot and perform a small song and dance routine in front my mother. She was impressed and decided to convey my demands to my father. He was in a good mood and agreed. And thus we were presented with 4 pieces of Samosas, my sister reaping the rewards of my hard-work. There was no chutney on the side, which was actually a relief. I hadn't forgotten the dream yet, albeit the mental scar was quickly replaced by the sight in my hands.

I took my piece and gobbled half of it in one bite. But wait, there was something wrong. I couldn't feel the softness of the tangy potatoes. Instead I felt something crunchy within my mouth. I took a piece out. Onions!? I looked at the other half of Samosa in my hand. Only onions!!! The travesty didn't end in my dream. I was living the nightmare!

My friends back in Bihar were right after all. This really was a completely foreign land. My friends, if they deserved to be called that, took a lot of enjoyment in describing the way my life was going to be turned upside down in Bangalore. Even the name sounded like nothing I had heard in my respectable life experience of 10 years. They all seemed very knowledgeable on the subject and specially so in the matters of food.

"They cook everything in coconut oil!"

"Forget about eating your favorite food, now it's all going to be coconut dishes fried in coconut oil and served with a side of coconut chutney!"

It were these conversations that were tormenting my dreams. I hoped that they were exaggerating. However my first experience of Samosa in South India had made me doubt my optimism. After all, I had expected the recipe for Samosa to transcend the borders of States and countries. With these thoughts in my mind I myself transcended the border of Karnataka from Tamilnadu and moved closer to the place, where I would be spending the next decade of my life.

We reached Bangalore late at night. I was woken up from yet another one of my gastronomic nightmares. We got down at the Bangalore Cantonment railway station. I wondered if it had something to do with canteen and food but I was too sleepy to think about these things in detail. We got into an auto and left for our destination. It seemed that I was still half asleep as I could see roads blinking with lights in the center and at the sides. Surely this was the stuff of dreams. I didn't want to waste any effort in dreaming with my eyes open. Thus I closed my eyes and fell into a deep slumber.

I accompanied my father the next day to run some errands. We were to catch a bus from Ulsoor to Majestic. Making sure that I remember where our home was in case I get lost, he took me to a restaurant for lunch. I looked up at the menu searching for my favorite delicacy. It seemed apart from the spoken language, the language of the belly was also differed here. The only food item I could recognize was dosa, having eaten it once on our family trip to odisha around 1995. I gave up any hope of finding samosas among such foreign cuisines.

Dejected, I turned around. My father handed me a small paper coupon, with Rs 5 written on it. It really didn't seem like a good time to fool me with paper money. Before I could protest I saw the cashier having a whole book full of them and people happily exchanged money with these pieces of paper. Perhaps I would understand these rituals better when my school started and I was trained in the local behavior.

What are you waiting for? Go get the ice-cream before the queue gets long.

Oh so that's what it was for! I hurried along and joined the queue.

The operator, kept the cone under the nozzle of the machine and out came the cream. One turn, then another one on top, followed by a third. The stack seemed unstable, I was worried it would fall and I would get none. However he turned it around the fourth time and then detached the cream from the machine. All this for Rs 5!

Perhaps it wouldn't be so bad here in Bangalore after all.

wp:comment.wp:comment_content: Opens kids' mind to cultures beyond their own. I loved it, keep these stories coming. 👍

item.title: Rubble, Rain, Hot Tea and Spiritual Bliss
item.dc:creator: divyaprakashpoddar
item.content:encoded:
If you let go of expectation, more often than not you will be rewarded with a fulfilling experience. This holds true for movies ,books, life in general and as we'll see a bike trip in the Himalayas.

We weren't really sure where we would be going that sunday. Abhigna (ma femme, mon partenaire) suggested Kalpeshwar, a place I had no idea about. In fact for most of the places we visit, I rarely have any idea beforehand. I actually think that's a good thing and intend to keep it that way, as I am completely unaware of the things to expect and this makes the journey exciting not knowing what's lies ahead. However this time, my expectations were not neutral, they were in fact negative. Usually we would start early morning around 5-6 AM for any other place. However, we began this journey rather late, around 10 AM. The reason being the unwillingness to actually ride that far to a place we weren't really excited about. I was always looking forward to visit places high up in the mountains, where I could admire the peaks reaching for the stratosphere. However as Abhigna told me, this place was in a valley, Urgam valley to be exact. With the sole motivation of visiting one of the Panch Kedars, we started our journey.

It was a sunny day, though we had prepared ourselves for the unpredictable rains of the mountains and carried a poncho and raincoat with us. We decided to have breakfast on the way at a restaurant owned by one our colleagues of our college. He too was at the restaurant when we reached there. He told us about his experience of visiting Kalpeshwar. He made sure that he gave us enough warnings about the road to that place. The roads were just for namesake. They were actually paths lined with loose gravel and the occasional boulders, with very high gradients which only got worse when it rained. He himself had taken many a fall while riding up that road. Knowing my capabilities as a bike rider, this got me worried. I hoped he was just exaggerating and things wouldn't be so bad. It was only a matter of a few hours for my hopes to be dashed. But the hours leading up to that moment were enjoyable thanks to a bright and sunny day.

 

We knew we had to get Helang and then cross a bridge to begin the ascent on the road to Urgam thus starting the main part of out journey. In order to cross a river and get to the other mountain, you have to descend, cross the river on a bridge and then ascend again. It may be trivial for many people, but I only realized this once I started living in Gopeshwar. We didn't actually know, where on the highway the road that descended towards the river lay. Asking many people on the way, we were eventually sent along the right direction. On an earlier trip to Auli, I had seen the temple (Red monument near the center of the image below.) from the highway and asked my driver about it. He informed us that, that road is very treacherous and specially that turn. There had been so many accidents that locals had built a Lord Hanuman temple on the turn to protect the travelers. I did not know that one day I myself would be going down that same road.

We took the highway exit and started going down the road. The quality of the road had already started deteriorating and looking ahead it seemed that it would get much worse.

We descended on our side of the mountain and approached the bridge that would take us on the mountain on which the Pandavas had chosen to build one of the five temples dedicated to Almighty Neelkantha. Since the roads had worsened in quality as we approached the bridge, my capabilities as a biker was put to the test.

I failed the test as soon as it started. As we approached this bridge, I thought we should stop here to take a look at the roaring Alaknanda. However, not paying attention to the thick layer of silt on the road, I applied the brakes, the bike skidded and we both took a fall. Dazed and confused, we got up, picked up the bike and contemplated that maybe we should head back. After all I couldn't handle a simple change in terrain. But Abhigna had faith in me and she convinced that we should in fact continue since taking a fall at the starting itself would make me pay more attention on the roads to come. Up ahead, the Hanuman temple was visible. We prayed for protection proceeded towards the turn.

We took the turn and once again, both of this time, doubted if we should continue the journey. The road ahead was full of rubble and sloping upwards at a steep gradient. We were so tensed and worried about the upcoming ride that we didn't take any pictures. So you'll have to trust me when I say the road really was treacherous. If you ask around in Garhwal, you'll find many people agreeing with our views. Already having taken a fall in the beginning, I was filled with trepidation about the riding my bike. I went ahead with the bike engaged in the first gear. However the bike started slipping backwards because of the rubble. Maybe an experienced biker could have handled it better. Fearing a fall again, Abhigna decided that she would climb down and walk up the slope while I alone rode the bike. This we made the first part of our ascent. Just beyond the slope we heard a thundering sound.

We parked the bike and looked over the cliff, it turned out the sound was caused by water flowing in a big pipeline. It was most probably part of a small run off the river hydraulic power plant. The water was being discharged into a clear river that we later learned was called Kalpganga. We decided to head back up the road. By now the weather had changed and it seemed that rain would soon accompany us. We continued, riding very slowly and never going above second gear. We rode for about an hour.

The journey from there onward comprised of broken roads, roads filled with rubble, roads submerged by mini-waterfalls flowing down the mountain side, muddy roads. In short all the types of roads you could test your caliber as a mountain biker. Unfortunately I was neither a mountain biker nor was our bike a rough terrain bike. It was fun nonetheless. We approached dangerous parts of the road with a fast beating heart, and once we were through it, the adrenaline rush of the experience made the hardship count.

Finally we reached a place, where there were other cars, jeeps, parked on the side of the road. Asking around, people told us that the road ahead is not drivable. Thus it seemed we would have to walk. We regretted having not started early. It was already quite late and walking would cost us more time. I was also fearing our way back. The path also passed through jungles and I felt scared thinking of the consequences of having to drive down that treacherous road in the dark. But since we had reached so close, there was no turning back and we decided to continue.

We parked the bike on the side of the road and began our walk. One of the many wonderful things about Uttarakhand is the nature of their people. In any other place I would have been worried about leaving bike parked in an isolated spot, where anyone if they wanted could have broken the lock and rode off. However, my experience of living here for the last few months comforted me and I knew the locals could be trusted and my bike would remain there unharmed even if I came back after a few days.

The sky was beginning to darken and we didn't really know how far ahead the temple was. The path turned a corner and soon we were walking through a jungle. It had begun to drizzle lightly, but we were protected under the cover of trees. After a few minutes walk, tress gave way and we were greeted with the views of a beautiful waterfall, falling from a tremendous height. It seemed that all our troubles would be worth it. However, this was only an introduction of the things to come. We would soon be rewarded with many more surprises.

We paused for some time and admired the waterfall. At first we thought that the small white structure seen in the image below was the temple for which we were destined. This worried us instantly. We were certainly not prepared for such a steep climb.

Walking a few more steps showed us the path of our true destination. Although the place itself wasn't visible yet, we were welcomed by the Uttarakhand Tourism signboard, acquainting us with the history of the temple and its other important facts. We decided to rest for a few minutes and take some pictures. After all the temple couldn't have been much further away from the Tourism signboard.

We took off soon as we were eager to reach the temple. After a few minutes, we could see the temple on the other side of a small gorge. However there was a minor problem. It seemed that there was no means to get to the other side.

The bridge that would allow us to cross the river, Kalpganga flowing in the gorge was devastated. Another means of crossing, a small cable car, was also abandoned. It had also started raining heavily and we needed to get to the temple soon.

Walking a bit further, showed us a path that descended down to the river. It was then that we could see a makeshift bridge of logs and chains on a part of river where it was the narrowest.

Out of excitement and in order to get shelter from the rain, both of us made a run for the bridge. However once on the bridge, we stopped for a few minutes to admire the river and take a few pictures.

We could also see the waterfall closely but we decided to visit it on the way back. Now we had to go back up the gorge. We started looking for a path and in a few minutes realized that no well defined path existed.

We knew the only way up was on a steep muddy slope made slippery now due to the heavy downpour. Helping each other we made our way up slowly and steadily.

It took us some time but eventually we made it to the top without any mishap. The rains had intensified and we ran inside the temple seeking shelter. A priest seemed to be waiting for us and welcomed us wholeheartedly. He asked to take off our ponchos and raincoats and leave them on the corner to dry. He requested us to take some rest and when ready to follow him to the small cave within which lay the holy Shivalinga.

We were exhausted so we sat down for a while, resting and drying ourselves. The place seemed magical and heavenly. The temple was almost empty of visitors. In fact apart from a few sadhus in a hut next to the temple, we couldn't spot anyone else. It seemed we three, us and the priest, were the only ones in the temple and this gave us a very special feeling. The dark clouds had transformed the sky and the heavy sound of rain and of the rapidly flowing Kalpganga below the temple gave us an experience of bliss never felt before. I haven't forgotten that experience till date and revisit that time in my memories quite often.

After a few minutes rest, we followed the priest to the sanctum sanctorum within the cave. It is hard to put into words, but the feeling of being inside the cave surrounded by diyas and flowers and The Shivalinga in the center along with other deities while thunder roared and heavy rain lashed the roof was exceptional and spiritual. The cave provided the much needed warmth and all our tiredness left us, while our mind became calm and our hands folded in reverence to the mighty Byomkesh and his hair (Jata) engraved in the stones above him for which the temple is named. We performed the puja, guided by the priest. He applied a thick paste of Sandalwood paste across our foreheads in the process. The aroma and the coolness of the paste soothed our minds.

Being from the city, my mind has been corrupted mostly because of bad experiences. While the Puja was going on, in my mind wandered the thought, that since the priest was so sincerely performing the Puja, he must be expecting a good amount of dakshina once it was over. I had learnt to expect to haggle with priests in temples and thus my expectations were the same. However, this wasn't the case here. The priest performed the Puja as part of his duty and didn't seem to expect anything in return. I handed him some money and he took it with gratitude hardly paying any attention to its amount. The people living in the difficult to reach places of Uttarakhand have been spared the cunningness that infects the city folks living in the plains.

We started a conversation with the Priest regarding the bridge, and he informed us that the bridge had collapsed during the floods of Uttarakhand in 2013. He invited us for a tea at his dwelling and we gladly agreed. He laid down some mats on the balcony outside his room and invited us to rest while he prepared tea inside. In a few minutes he was back with steaming tea for the three of us and we sipped and chatted away taking in the surroundings and hoping to carry this moment in our hearts forever.

The priest suggested that we should stay the night at a rest-house in the village since it was getting late and we may have trouble reaching home on time. However, we had a job to get back to as the next day was Monday. Also there wasn't anyway to inform our home owners that we wouldn't be back at night. From the moment we entered the path to Urgam valley, our phones were devoid of any signal. Thus with no other option available we decided to head back. We also wanted to spend sometime at the waterfall so we took the leave of the priest, prayed one last time at the temple and descended down the dilapidated path.

Soon after getting down, we headed for the waterfall. Water was flowing rapidly down the slick black rocks and spraying us, thus drenching us even more. We wandered around the fall, listening to its thunderous sounds and posing for a few pictures.

We also spent some time inspecting the ruins of the destroyed cable bridge. The river must have overflowed to quite some height for it to be able to destroy the bridge completely. Throughout Uttarakhand you can still see remnants of the destruction caused by the 2013 floods. We took some more pictures for memories and then hurriedly made our way up the gorge on the other side.

We walked quickly as the light had started dimming. However in this low light we could clearly see some of the snow capped peaks sparkling up ahead. We thanked the gods for opening up the skies just enough to allow us these otherworldly vistas.

We came to the place where we parked the bike and sure enough it was right where we left it. We got on the bike and took some more pictures and then finally bid the place goodbye.

The path back was covered without any unusual incidents. However there is one thing which clearly stood out in the last part of the journey. While descending down the mountain as we approached a hairpin bend, an exquisite scene presented itself to us, almost like a parting gift. The whole of Urgam was visible with high snow capped mountains in the background. It felt magical. I regretted not having brought my DSLR camera. I wanted to capture it in as much details as possible. I did what I could with my phone camera.

We wanted to stop for a bit longer but the approaching night worried us and we soon got back on the bike and continued our return journey.

We reached the lord Hanuman temple on the treacherous bend and stopped there for a while to appreciate the confluence of Kalpganaga and Alaknanda. The river Alaknanda meets many such companions on its way and finally takes the identity of Ganga after meeting Bhagirathi in Devprayag.

While we were admiring the views, we saw another person nearby who seemed like he was from the army. Upon inquiring he confirmed our assumption. He had stopped there to perform Puja in the temple. We joined him and thanked lord Hanuman for keeping us safe throughout the journey. Apart from the fall at the beginning, there had been no other untoward incidents. We took one last parting picture with the bike next to the temple and crossed the Alaknanda river to head back home to Gopeshwar having a stomach devoid of any food and a mind filled with memories.

After almost a year we went back to the same place with my parents. We had no difficulty crossing the gorge this time.

item.title: The Casual Hike
item.dc:creator: divyaprakashpoddar
item.content:encoded:
Many of us had returned back to Gopeshwar after visiting our home towns during the summer vacation of our institute. We were desperately looking forward to an outing. The plan was to go on a casual hike, or so we thought. On the eve of our planned hike ominous clouds had started appearing in the sky. We hadn't had a proper visit to the mountains in a couple of months thus the prospect of rains dampened our spirits.

Hiking during rainy weather in the mountains is a dangerous affair due to occurrences of flash floods, landslides, thunder strikes (rare but still a possibility in high up places). The last few days had been dry and thus it irritated us to think that the clouds had chosen to shed their weight now. With nothing else to do but hope we signed off for the night, woken up a few times by the ear-splitting sound of thunder (It gets really loud in the mountains). Unknown to us, rains of this night were busy transforming the rivers and creeks of Mandal into a sight to behold.

We were delighted the next morning to see clear skies all around. We thanked our good fortune and got ready quite quickly so that we could start as early as possible. Our hiking party consisted of 5 people, including me and Abhigna. Three of our friends were to accompany us, Lijo, Lijin and Avinash. Their homes were at an elevation of about 400 m below ours, closer to the Alaknanda river. They showed up on time as planned on a hired vehicle and picked us up. We all proceeded towards Mandal village, the place from where the hike to Anusuya Devi Temple starts.

I was fortunate to capture the entire trek route, from Mandal village to the temple, while coming down from Rudranath in October 2019. Apart from the places in this blog, one can also see Chandrashila peak (4000 m above sea level), home of the highest Shiva temple in the world, Tunganath. I have some wonderful memories of these places too which I'll share in my upcoming posts.

We were dropped off at the gates of Ma Anusuya Devi Temple. It's right on the roadside. However the actual temple is quite a hike away. Our Driver, Govind Bhai, our go to guy for any vehicle requirements, told us to be back soon. Taking our Non-pahadiness in to account, he expected us to be back at around 3-4 PM. We walked a few minutes down a road and wondered why didn't our driver just continue on it.

However only a few meters ahead, the road crossed a river on a bridge and ended abruptly on the other side. Amused by the strange sight, I turned to my friends to inquire what they though of it and found all of them staring not at the bridge but its background.

Innumerable waterfalls were reflecting the morning sun along the side of the mountain. This could have been only possible because of the heavy rains last night. The rains had emptied the clouds reducing them to wisps, leaving the sky a shade of blue which could only have come from a painter's pallet. All the rain water was now flowing along the sides of mountain atop which the temple stood. We started counting the number of waterfalls but soon gave up realizing the futility of our efforts. Not only was it pointless to count them, in the process we were missing the precious moments of this wonderful scene conjured up for us by the rain gods. We happily just admired them for a while and it was quite some time before any of us started moving again.

We got on the path, and went through the village. The old style pahadi homes are really small, even though they are two storied, probably to keep the warmth inside. We came across a mini waterfall on the way and it seemed. We got so excited that we spent quite some time adoring it and clicking pictures around it. We had no idea that this did not represent even a small percentage of what was in store for us.

We continued on the path, being led by a buffalo for sometime, she seemed to wait for us if we stopped. Or perhaps she was wondering why we were following her.

We kept walking ahead, always under the shadow of the sheer wall in front of us, atop which lay our destination. Strangely it seemed intimidating and awe-inspiring simultaneously.

We walked on the path with a jungle on one side and the rapidly flowing river on the other. At many places, waterfalls from our left side fell down from the forests and went under and across our path to join the river on our right.

Every now and then we paused and looked at each other conveying the blissful state of our minds through our gaze. Everyone one us seemed genuinely happy and it showed in the springiness of our steps along the hilly gradients.

A kilometer or so further down the route, a small path descended sideways. This was the opportunity that we had been heartily seeking. Without any hesitation we all descended down the path and came to rocky banks of the river.

The river was split into two parts by a pile of boulders. The roughly flowing rapids went one way, away from us, while a calm, narrow stream gently flowed towards us. We all went down to this stream and dipped our feet in it's cold and fresh waters.

Me and Lijo climbed up a few boulders and took pictures of the scary part of the river. The other bank of the river was held in place by a steep, almost vertical mountain side. Many waterfalls adorned this rocky wall and joined the river.

We all sat down each occupying a personal boulder and lost ourselves in the calmness of the noisy river. I can't recall a moment in my life when I have been this close to my spiritual self and have felt such happiness.

My mind completely satiated after feasting on nature's visual and aural platter, it was time to listen to my envious and empty stomach's growls. It had been quite some time since we last had anything to eat. We walked once again, keeping an eye out for any place offering food to the pilgrims. We didn't have to walk long. There was a hut just after crossing the river which had food as well a lodging facilities (a cozy bed and some blankets).

We ordered the staple mountain food for hikers, a hot plate of Maggi, along with chai (obviously!). We walked about the bridge and taking some pictures and talking with the shopkeepers. The sun was was now shining directly on us, making us seek shade under the hut's canopy. The day had started to become humid and that meant that rains would probably greet us in the latter part of the day.

Sensing the upcoming rainy weather, we quickly gobbled up our breakfast and got back on the ever upward sloping path on this side of the bridge. We even came across a few leeches on the path, and did our best to stay clear of them. Many a times we would hear sound of streams and water falling just beyond the canopy of trees. However, we had to resist our temptation to go looking for them as we were now getting a bit late and we also had the prospects of rains to worry about.

Along the way we came across native women carrying huge stacks of grass on their backs. The mountain ladies are very strong and do most of the physically demanding household work. In Gopeshwar I had seen women carrying up to two gas cylinders on their shoulders and walking up on a steep road, whereas I struggled to carry an empty cylinder up the steps of my home. Impressed and admiring the grit of these women, we continued forward.

The weather changed, as predicted, for the rest of the journey. Heavy rains ensued and forced us to take shelter. The rains didn't last long though and soon we were back on track. I had my first encounter with a leech in my life. Fortunately I pried it off me, before it could take a proper hold. We stopped momentarily at many places and took many pictures mentally and with our cameras. After about two hours of continuous hiking since breakfast, we finally reached the first part of our destination.

Being the only ones at temple, we were welcomed and greeted by the priest. We prayed for a while inside the temple. It seemed we would be the last ones to arrive for the day, as the priest closed the temple doors soon after we were done praying. We went outside and started walking around the courtyard. Mountains and clouds surrounded us in all directions.

I looked up at the sky and wondered which obscured mountains lay beyond the clouds. I was unaware that my future self was looking back at me from one of those mountain tops, through his camera lens.

The priest looked over at us and seemed to discuss something with his colleague. He then came over and asked us if we were going further ahead on the route towards Atri Muni Ashram . We replied in affirmative. He then hopefully asked us if we could do a small favor for him, to which we readily agreed. He then handed me a bag full of Tulasi leaves and told us that this has been requested by a sage living in the forest along the way and we are supposed to make the delivery. He gave a brief description of his hut so that we could spot it from the path.

After a brief visit to the lord Dattatreya, Anusuya Devi's son in a nearby temple, we continued the journey towards his father Atri muni's Ashram. Although the priest at the temple had warned us about the paths being flooded due to the recent rains, we wanted to see it for ourselves. More importantly, we now also had a delivery job to complete.

We walked along always keeping an eye out for any match to the description of the sage's hut given to us. The hut supposedly had a blue tarp placed on its roof, to protect it from the rains. We spotted it after a while down the slope on the right side of the road. Eager to meet the sage, we all excitedly went down the wet pathway strewn with leaves and the occasional leech trying with all its might to attach itself to some living creature.

"How many of you are there?"
He peeked outside, did a mental head count and seemed hopeful. "Would you guys care to join me for a task that's been pending for some time?"
Why not? We thought. How often do you get to help an ascetic in a jungle? We all agreed although I couldn't help wondering what the task actually was. We were withheld this information and just asked to follow him down a slope. He said he'll just show us instead of explaining. He thanked us for the Tulasi leaves and kept the bag inside his hut. He then put on his sandals and led us deeper into the forest. After walking for a few minutes through the forest we started to hear a familiar sound and it seemed that we would soon be approaching another waterfall. I wondered what task the sage had in his mind. I hoped that he had not overestimated our capabilities. The lush green and wet forest ended and we emerged at a set of stairs leading down to the source of a heart penetrating sound.

In front of us mother nature had laid out a scene much sought after by cameramen of those "Planet Earth" documentaries. A rapid, untamed river flowed down the mountain on our left and then past a makeshift wooden log bridge on our right, and fell into unknown depths again, the cliffs reverberating its sound in the forest.

For the umpteenth time, it again seemed that the beauty of the scene we were witnessing couldn't be surpassed. But we had been proven wrong on all the earlier occasions and none of us were complaining. After cherishing the scene to our full satisfaction we looked at our guide. He wasn't in the lead anymore. He had gone up a path on our left, towards a gated cave, which seemed to be the manifestation of a mountain lovers dream home.

It turned out to be his home during the summer months. The place became risky to stay during monsoons because of the fear of flash floods. He soon came out of the cave-home with some tools and led us to the bridge. It was there that he briefed us on our mission.

A driftwood which was basically a large tree root was stuck under the bridge. This gave leverage to the fast flowing water behind it and the bridge was in danger of being pushed from its anchor points, down the river and into the waterfall up ahead. His plan was to use a log or some tool as a lever and try to lift the bridge from one side above its anchor point. This should provide enough space for the driftwood to flow underneath the bridge and solve our problems.

There was another small cave nearby, in which wooden logs were stored. He directed us to take one from there and use it as a lever to lift the bridge. After going through some of the inventory, we decided on a log and carried it to the bridge.

He placed a large rock near the bridge to act as a fulcrum. We put one end of the log into a crevice under the bridge and over the rock and pushed with all our might down the other end. The log snapped! We should have expected that. The bridge was bulky. We were then handed an iron rod, supplied from the cave, and got back to work.

Eventually our effort paid off and the bridge moved just enough for the stuck root to flow under it. Filled with sense of accomplishment, we all celebrated. The sage told us that the bridge had been built by him along with the help of the local villagers and thus it was very dear to him. Very pleased with us, he invited us for a cup of tea in his home. We all happily obliged.

All that time spent in strenuous work justified some moments to be spent in vanity and thus we took turns posing next to our accomplished work.

We spent a few more moments relaxing next to the river. The way forward to Atri Muni's Ashram was blocked due to the overflowing streams and thus we were advised not go ahead. We all were too exhausted anyway, thus we decided to come back again some other day. Before leaving, we all posed for a selfie.

The sage laid out mats for us inside his hut and took out a tetra pack of milk and some biscuits. He explained that the nearby villagers and pilgrims on this route regularly supply his ration out of devotion and respect. It must really take some guts to live this deep in the jungles, year after year. While the water boiled, we all introduced ourselves to babaji. As for his introduction, it surprised us when he revealed that he was an accomplished eye surgeon. However, he had left it all behind him and was living blissfully in the lap of mother nature for past many years.

The tea was ready and he offered it to all of us along with a platter of biscuits. We had a long discussion with him on arbitrary topics and in the process gained a quite some wisdom, however you'll have to climb up the mountain yourself if you want to aquire it. (Actually, I am saving that for another post. :] ). Soon it was time to leave. He thanked us for all our help, and made one last request. He had a few solar panels to take care his lighting needs at night. However the inverter battery had run out of electrolyte. He asked us to inform a shopkeeper in Gopeshwar about this. The shopkeeper was a regular on this route and would deliver the battery-water to him on his next trip. We finally bid goodbye and left for Mandal.

On our way back Abhigna slipped on the wet, stone path. It seemed that she might have sprained her ankle which was worrisome because we had almost the entire route left to cover. However the fall turned out to be a blessing in disguise. In order to check the damage, she removed her sandals and shockingly found out that two leeches had been been happily sucking blood on her foot for the past who knows how many hours. We had encountered some leehes on the floor in babaji's hut and he had sprinkled salt on them to keep them at bay. We didn't expect babaji's wisdom to come to our help so soon. We looked around and saw a shop next to the temple. One of us quickly went and brought some salt and sprayed it on Abhigna's feet. The leeches soon loosened their grip and we were finally able to get rid of them. Checking all our shoes, sandals, shirts and pants thoroughly for leeches we again descended down the pathway.

Our driver was worried sick, since it was almost 6 PM when we finally reached his vehicle. He had asked people going up the mountain to look for us and had given them our description. He feared that we had been washed away in one of the overflowing streams like some tourists a few years ago. As compensation (maybe not according to him) we gave him a detailed account of all the adventures we had been a part of on our way back home.

item.title: English Confusion
item.dc:creator: divyaprakashpoddar
item.content:encoded:
My first encounter with English and its accompanying confusions started in the toilet.
"It's an English Toilet", my father informed me.
I wondered what purpose it served, since I sat the same way I did in my normal toilet in Bihar. The daily ascent to the top required a lot of effort. If anything this was more discomforting. I added this to the rapidly growing list things I would ask my local friends, the ones I was yet to make.

The problem with making friends was that they all spoke English.
"'Come da, lets play!"' Raghvendra said, welcoming me in his group.
I did understand bits and pieces. I had had an epiphany regarding "da". One of the things I was grateful for, once I moved here was the pre-installed cable wire at our home. Our Black and White TV had a dial that rotated about 12 times, and it had never been rotated before coming to Bangalore. One of those rotations was a gateway to a world of cartoons. A complete channel dedicated only to cartoons. It didn't matter if they all spoke in English. I had gotten more than I dreamed for and I didn't want to be greedy lest these be taken away. So anyway, there was this cartoon show in which there was a talking rabbit. I hardly understood any of his dialogues, but he always seemed to end his sentences with a 'da'. So perhaps that was the inspiration for these kids. Pretty impressed by myself I congratulated myself on making this connection.
"ok da", I replied mimicking the bunny.

Following along my "potential friends" for a few hours didn't seem to incite much response from them as I was unable to be part of their communication. I retired to my home and switched on the TV to meet my comprehension-less but entertaining friends on Cartoon Network. It had only been a few days since we moved here and the TV screen had started to become blurry. Perhaps it couldn't handle the overload of 12 channels. I moved my chair closer to the TV and immersed myself in a scene in which a doctor poured some chemicals into a pot and began stirring it.

"Shame! Shame!"
I turned around and saw our neighbor in the next building calling out to me. Although I had a slight idea about the meaning (the words was similar to 'Sharm' in Hindi), the disapproving look on her face confirmed it. She then got into a conversation with my mother probably complaining to her about my TV watching habits and eye damage in mixed Tamil and English while my mother nodded along and uttered a few words of agreement in Hindi.

I thought to myself, if someone should be ashamed then it should be her, as most morning she smuggled water (Bore water, a rare commodity in Bangalore) from our house, through a pipe hidden under laundry . However, I remembered the delicious Idly and Vada she gave usually gave us in exchange and thus forgave her.

My school started within a few days after shifting to Bangalore. My father decided to drop me there on my first day. The way to school was quite fascinating. There were broad roads, and even broader pathways on the sides, perhaps that's why some motorists preferred driving on them every now and then. It seemed way more fun than riding on the road and I decided to ask my father to take that path the next time.

We passed a movie theater, named LIDO. I could see a ''coming soon'' poster of a movie ''Spider-Man'' on it. The person in the poster resembled my favorite superhero"Nagraj" but he had web coming out of his wrist instead snake-ropes. Thus it seemed "Nagraj" too was transformed when he moved down south. Or , Maybe the one in the poster was an evil twin with similar powers. Curious about finding more, I added the movie it to the list of things I would nag my father for over the coming weekend.

My gaze, along with the scooter moved to the buildings next to the theater. The buildings seemed newly constructed but I wondered why had they constructed only toilets on it. No only that, the English versed people of Bangalore had even got the spelling wrong. Each of the multiple boards on the building read "To--Let". Giving it more thought, I finally concluded that the letter I of the printing press may have rotated sideways by mistake and printed all these boards wrong.

We soon came to a junction of roads.
"It's called the Trinity Circle", my father informed me.
Confused, I reasoned that the local geometry books must have also undergone geographical changes like the Samosa's recipe. However my train of thoughts was derailed by the sight of some of the tallest buildings I had seen in my life at the "Corners" of the Trinity "Circle."

There was a building on our left which had a board of "Vijaya Bank" at the top. There were two grayish building in our front that resembled the ones in English TV shows I had managed sneak a glance while quickly changing channels. I was impressed. We took a left turn and proceeded towards my school.

Once I got off the scooter at my school, I got showered with instructions.
"Hail an Auto-Rickshaw."
"Tell him "Hanumaiah Reddy Road, Ulsoor!
"Don't forget to say, Meter!"
"To any of his questions, simply reply, "Kannada Gotilla!' "
"Give him Rs. 7 once you reach home."
Equipping me with the above knowledge and the moolah, My father left me at the gates of my school.

Standing at the gates,I went over the dialogues in my mind a millionth time.
"Hi"
"How are you?"
I decided I may throw in a "Dude" or "Man" here and there (Fresh knowledge from the cartoons.)
I entered the class and rushed to the empty seat at the back. I didn't want to sit at the front being exposed to the teacher's questions in English. There were two other students sitting next to my seat and they all turned towards me at once. I gulped and quickly revised the greetings and questions in my head. My struggle with English for the past few days had made me very nervous. Almost trembling, I changed my script at the last second and instead asked them hesitatingly.
"You know Hindi?"
"Haan", they replied.

"Haan?" What does that mean?? I hadn't come across this word in English yet. I tried to recall all the words which I had recently heard but couldn't find a match. Was it the accent which deluded me or were they mocking me? Before I could reply with my ready-made dialogues, it dawned on me that it was Hindi that they were speaking.

I gave a sigh of relief and forgot all about my prepared lines. I improvised in Hindi and greeted them all and inquired about their well-beings. Finally having found friends I could talk to, I joyfully looked forward to my first day at school in Bangalore.

wp:comment.wp:comment_content: Yes…. journey is beautiful indeed… the way you explained your first encounter with English is really interesting and literally I was travelling through your way to school … though I have never been there…yes we have talked sometime…and i am glad to read your work… fascinating story 👌
I love the way you take the Readers through your journey. It almost feels like witnessing everything in front of yourself! Great work!

item.title: Slippery Slopes
item.dc:creator: divyaprakashpoddar
item.content:encoded:
It was our first trip as a group. All of us had gathered at Gopeshwar from different parts of India. We had representatives from Haryana, Uttakrakhand, Bihar, Gujarat, Kerala. We were sent here to teach at a local Engineering college, but the benefits of this job were beyond just academic satisfaction. However, we were yet to make use of these benefits, as the intial days of our job were spent in office work. So this was the first trip we all had finally agreed upon.

The place was Chopta, a popular destination among tourists. We had also plans of hiking all the way upto the Tungnath Temple and finally to the Chandrashila summit. Although the plans were in contrast to our physical abilities.

item.title: German se Ladai Aur Rudranath ki Chadhai
item.dc:creator: divyaprakashpoddar
item.content:encoded:
With my mind wandering every night to the Uttarakhand mountains, staying away was unbearable. It had been one whole year since our transfer to Jorhat, Assam but we were still engulfed in the charm of the Himalays. We finally decided on a trek/pilgrimage to Rudranath, climbing which was as difficult as defeating the Germans. ( I am not making this up! The title of the post is a popular saying among the residents of the villages nearby Rudranath). We made the plan as perfect as we could. This was one of the rare trips where everything fell into place (almost), and we could do things as we planned.

The plan was for a 3-day trek starting from Sagar Village. We planned to return using a different route than the one used for ascending. However, that depended on whether we could find a few more trekkers on the way who would be descending down the same path. The reason was that the path was through a dense forest.

We arrived at Haridwar station and got on the bus to Gopeshwar. Just after passing Rishikesh, my memories and the images from my dreams in the previous year started materializing on our bus windows.

On my right, the river Ganga had taken on a golden hue. The morning sun filtering through the clouds in the valley made the whole scene surreal. I felt myself descend into tranquility as once again I journeyed into the land of the gods, Devbhoomi Uttarakhand. Passing the famous prayags (confluence) of the river Alaknanda one by one we reached Gopeshwar by evening. Our hosts were our house owners. We were so grateful to them for inviting us to stay in the same place where we had accrued so many memories.

Waking up, the first thing I did was to run upto the terrace and look for the scene I had missed all year long. The river Alaknanda flowing through the valley, passing next to the college where we taught for almost a year. The sun illuminated the college building, intensifying the nostalgia. This view is forever imprinted into my brain.

We got up early. Our trekking partners, Lijo and Lijin too had reached Gopeshwar the previous day from Pantnagar. They were supposed to meet us on the road. Our hosts were generous enough to get up even before us and prepare our lunch for the trek. All of them came up to road to bid us goodbye. They wished us luck, although some doubted our capabilities. The Sumo soon came to meet us with our friends inside. We got on and started towards Sagar village, on the route we drew and erased so many times on our whiteboard in Assam.

We left some of our extra luggage on a hotel in Sagar. We had planned to stay at that hotel when we returned. Our driver suggested that we carry walking sticks with us. The hotel people were generous enough to give us a stick each with the promise that we return them on our way back. After a selfie on the entrance to trek we started on a journey to collect memories.

Although the sun had come up, a mountain separated us from its greetings. It was probably good as we could cover more ground when the sun wasn't directly shining upon us. We quickly made our way through the village. We needed to ask a few locals about which of the many paths to take that would lead us to the foot of the mountain towering ahead, which we needed to scale. The temple was on the other side of the mountain further along the ridge.

We found our first stop just after about 10-15 minutes of walking. This was the place where two paths leading to the main trek met. It was marked by a pratikshalaya (A waiting place). We rested there for some time and drank a glass of refreshing Buransh juice. There were a few others too, who were headed our way. Soon after finishing our drinks we filled our bottles from a stream nearby and started on the path ahead.

We soon reached our first pit stop, Pung bugyal. There we met a group of students from the college we used to teach at. They were from civil engineering and recognized Abhigna. They were all 'Pahadi' and were very quick on their feet. They greeted us and handed us candies which they were eating and sped up ahead. We decided to lay down, take rest and have our breakfast. We looked for a dry place to sit down. We found a stream nearby and filled our bottles. Finally settled we sat together in a circle and relished our breakfast. Our food from now on-wards depended on the lodging facilities at each of the three upcoming bugyals. They mostly had food, but the availability depended on the number of pilgrims visiting them on any given day. They had limited ration and even limited resources to carry ration up the mountain.

We were soon done with our breakfast and were quite content with the progress we had made thus far. We were packing our stuff, when we noticed a middle aged man walking returning from the trek up ahead. We asked him how much more distance was left to cover. He replied that you haven't even started. The climb up ahead was nothing compared to what we had done till now. The real climb started just beyond the bridge up ahead. That is when we actually set foot on the mountain to be climbed. We didn't waste much time after this and soon walked full speed ahead to the mountain up ahead.

We soon came across the bridge. The climb was indeed steep on the other side. The path was like this till Panar bugyal after which the way was comparatively easier. We had planned to spend our first night at Panar bugyal and thus had to reach there before sunset. Me and Abhigna had been preparing for this moment since the past 4-5 months. Hoping that our squats and lunges would pay off, we started excitedly on the strenuous part of our journey.

We walked continuously through the thick tree cover. On the way, we met some men with ponies who carried people up for a fee. They warned us that drinking water wouldn't be available till the next stop, Mauli Kharak. Thus, we were advised to fill our bottles with water from a stream just ahead. The water seemed to originate from under the roots of a tree and through some boulders. We quenched our thirst, replenished our bottles, and continued on our journey.

It was only after about a couple of hours that the shade of canopy ended and we were provided views of the path we had taken since morning. Looking closely, we were excited to identify a bald patch in the the forest as Pung bugyal. We were proud of ourselves for having covered so much distance. We took a break there for a few minutes.

We had used up almost all our water and the next stop, Mauli Kharak was still quite some time away. Thankfully we met a few people who were coming down and they happily offered us some water to drink. We inquired about the route ahead. They doubted that we would be able to reach Panar bugyal before sunset. The view at Panar is famously exquisite and we wanted that to be our reward for all the hard work we had done today. We headed quickly for Mauli kharak to gain some lost time.

The last bit of distance to Mauli Kharak was covered with a lot of complaints about hunger, thirst, tiredness, etc. We had been walking non-stop and desperately needed some rest. Thankfully, there was some food available at that place. we sat down on a few boulders, filled up our bottles from a nearby stream and relaxed. I took out my camera and hoped to capture some exotic birds, but a black crow sitting on a branch next to me held my gaze in a stare-down battle and eventually I had to capture him in my camera. On our way, there was a place called Pitradhar, where according to legends our ancestors visit in the form of crows. Remembering this bit of information, I respectfully removed my gaze and got back on track.

As dusk approached, our plan on reaching Panar before sunset started to seem impossible as all of us were extremely tired. Climbing for about an hour, we could see a grassland approaching. It was Luiti Bugyal.

We collapsed on the plastic chairs kept outside the stone hut and mutually agreed that it wouldn't be possible to cover any more distance today. The caretaker who was a friend of our house owner, welcomed us and offered us tea. And thus once again we relished the coveted pleasure of sipping tea in cold mountain weather while chatting with friends.

We took some photos of the wildlife. One of the most beautiful and elegant cows I have seen.

There was still some time for the sun to go down. Energized with tea and biscuits, me and Lijo decided to explore around and gather images with our cameras. Nearby we saw a bunch of cattle grazing, a dog, and his pup keeping guard. The puppy who was playing along with fawns had started to behave like one. It was one of the fluffiest puppies I had come across. I was a bit taken aback to see a thick metal collar with spikes around the guard dog, which seemed quite uncomfortable. I was informed that dogs need to be protected from Guldars(Mountain wild cats) as they attack the neck first. Taking a lot of pics and playing around with the puppy and fawns we headed back to the our hut as the sun neared the horizon.

The hut was split into two parts, with the kitchen in the middle. There were many beds laid on the floor for pilgrims. The floor itself was insulated from the cold ground by Styrofoam sheets. Overall, the place looked very cozy and comfortable to us tired souls.

We were hoping that apart from the four of us, it would be great if no one else came to our side of the hut. This wish was fulfilled as night approached, and no one else entered our home for the night. The caretaker got busy cooking dinner for us, and soon, on our plates, served some delicious food for the night. With the taste of heavenly hot food in cold mountain weather we were completely satiated.

The night was spent comfortably under the cozy blankets of which there was no shortage. We got up early the next morning as we had more than half the distance to cover. Also, we were eager to reach Panar, which was only about an hour's trek away. We took off soon after freshening up, gulping down the morning tea, and making the due payments.

The weather was cloudy on our way to the top. During our trek on this side of the mountain, we didn't see any snow-clad mountain peaks. They were all hidden behind the mountain we were climbing. As we started nearing the top, a glimpse of mighty Trishul excited us and energized our tired bodies. We wasted no time in completing the rest of the way to Panar.

I was walking ahead, and Abhigna was lagging behind. Unable to contain my excitement, I covered the last stretch quite quickly and came back to Abhigna even quicker to describe the amazing scenes I had witnessed.

We lay down on the lush green meadows, locally called bugyals. There were a few cows getting their breakfast fresh from the fields. A few tents were pitched down the hill. We were tempted to approach them for our morning tea, but we had to first take in all the scenes around us until we were satisfied.

Up until Panar, the path is quite steep. Locals call it 'khadi chadhai', literally meaning a vertical climb. The way ahead wasn't as strenuous. We prayed at the temple dedicated to forest gods and continued ahead. The mountain ranges visible from this side of the mountain had so much detail in them which lay obscured behind the ever shifting veil of clouds. Every few minutes we would turn and raise our heads in their direction and be surprised by the something previously unseen. A river flowing from the very top, through a deep valley was presented to us. It was one of the most memorable scenes.

We walked for about a couple of hours on the ridge of the mountain, meeting people on their way back and always asking the same question. "Aur kitni door?" Clouds accompanied us on this part of the trek and offered us mesmerizing views each time they cleared, much like a magician revealing whats behind his veil.

The next stop on our map was Pitradhar. Here we had to cross the ridge from one side of the mountain to the other. There was sort of a gateway constructed on this pass and the view on the other side was again spectacular. However this time we focused more on our growling stomachs and quickly ordered some food. But we were late, and the food had almost runout, there were only two aloo parathas left along with some rice and local daal. We took what we could get. The steaming hot dal and chawal was as delicious as one could hope for at this high altitude place at almost 4000m above sea level.

This was the highest point in our journey. For the next few hours we had to walk down a gentle slope towards another pit stop, panch ganga. Five individual streams flowed there, that's why the name. Tiredness was setting in and we hoped to reached our next resting spot soon.

We didn't take long to reach panchganga. There are lodging facilities there for travelers. We sat down for a few minutes but we had to get back on track soon as evening was approaching quickly and we had to reach Rudranath soon to secure our bed at the final camp. The path meandered behind a mountain ahead and no matter how much we walked, the path always seemed to turn around the corner.

The last bit was quite difficult. However as we turned a corner, we came at "Dev Darshini". It's the first point from where the temple is visible. You ring the bell and let the Shivji know that you're on your way.

The sun had started to set and we went down the slope towards the last part of out journey. We reached our final stay at about 6:30 PM. We quickly enquired for a room for four. We were shown to a room filled with blankets. Content with it we soon refreshed ourselves a bit and headed towrads the Lord's abode.

We wanted to be a part of the evening aarti, thus we quickly climbed up the steps to the temple. It started raining a bit, and we took shelter under a shed until the head priest came. We followed him inside the temple and he started with preparations for the aarti. There were about 10-15 people in total. All of us prayed and thanked lord Rudranath for letting us visit his pristine and serene abode.

We got back to our stay and had a sumptous, hot and steaming dinner. The chapati and vegetables put in our plates directly from the oven. Soon after finishing my dinner. I took out my tripod and setup my camera to take some night shots of the mountains surrounding Rudranath.

Having finally caught some sleep after shivering from the bone chilling cold most of the night, I started dreaming of the incredible vistas I had seen during the day. In dreams, one’s subconscious usually comes up with images which are fantasy but obviously my brain had difficulty conjuring up images any better than the one it had already seen the previous day. Thus all I could see in my dreams were the beautiful pathways I had trodden all day. These images seemed as unbelievable as they did during the day as they did in my sleep.

The dream ended and I woke up happily, completely aware of the fact that apart from my eyes being open now, nothing else has changed. I got out of the layers of (Heavy) blankets and opened the door of our stone house which had kept the insides relatively warm. Stepping outside in the cold morning, the sight in front of me stirred a primal fear within. The sight of sharp and tall, humongous mountains forming an inescapable wall on the horizon intimidated me. Being afraid was the last feeling I had expected to encounter in such a divine place. I felt imprisoned.

However fear turned into astonishment as my brain started processing the shapes of each of these peaks. I realized that I was being offered views of all the mountain peaks which had eluded me the earlier day. There it was the mighty Nanda Devi, the second tallest peak in India and then Brahmkamal and also Dronagiri and wait there was Trishul too! All presenting their silhouettes with the sun rising behind them. I had been in Uttarakhand for almost a year (and been to Auli thrice!) but hadn’t been deemed worthy of a glimpse of Nanda Devi peak. However climbing all the way to Rudranath must have convinced the weather gods to bestow upon me this wonderful view!

We climbed the steps again to the temple to seek blessings for our return journey. The early morning was almost as cold as night.

According to our plan on the whiteboard, we wanted to take the route to Ansuya Mata Temple and climb down the other side of the mountain. However we couldn't find any companions on the way. Our friends too had to take mules back to sagar as they had developed sores in their legs. The planned route was through a forest area and thus it would have been dangerous for just the two of us. Eventually we decided that we would retrace our path to sagar.

We had planned to reach sagar on the same day, but our legs couldn't keep with our mind's resolve and thus when we relaxed at Panar, we decided that the furthest we would hike today would be till Mauli Kharak. After Panar, we started climbing down the face of the mountain and reached Luiti Bugyal in about an hour. There we were informed that a large group had recently left for Mauli Kharatk and thus chances of finding a stay there were slim. Therefore, we decided to end our journey for the day at the stone hut of Luiti. However, the same night we found out that the stone hut wasn't so solid after all.

No one else arrived at our stay after us and thus we had the entire hut to ourselves. There was the owner who was also the cook and he prepared a sumptuous meal for us while his wood fired stove kept the entire hut quite warm. Content and tired we soon retired to our mattresses and crawled under warm and heavy blankets.

Flashes of lightning and thunderous sounds woke us up. We felt droplets of water spray across our faces. We both looked up and saw that part of the roof was flapping and the howling wind and rain was leaking through. Just outside, the owner was struggling to keep the flaps in place by the heavy stones which made up the wall.

Admist the heavy rain and hail, the owner managed to somehow tuck back the flaps under the stones . We couldn't sleep and waited for the storm to end. When it did end, we all took a peak outside. The storm had made the sky clear as a crystal and the night cold as ice. I envied the people who had decided to spend the night at Panar bugyal. The clear sky would have granted them heavenly views of the surrounding peaks reflecting the moonlight. Having been blessed with wonderful views through the trek, I guess I couldn't complain much.

We woke up early and freshened up soon. After a glass of scalding cup of chai, we started descending down the face of the mountain. We soon arrived at Mauli Kharak and realized that we were right in our decision to stay and Luiti the previous night. The number of people who had camped at Mauli Kharak were quite a few and it would've definitely been a crowded affair at the camps.

The rest of the climb down was without many incidences. We took about 5 more hours to reach Pung Bugyal, our first stop while climbing up. After resting there, we started again and reached Sagar in a couple of hours.

Looking back at the mountain, we still couldn't believe we accomplished the tasks that we had planned for months ahead. We proudly celebrated being deemed capable of taking on the Germans in battle!

item.title: Kite Season
item.dc:creator: divyaprakashpoddar
item.content:encoded: Couldn't try to cut other's kite as even a single one was hard to come by. In the morning while I was brushing my teeth a kite far away in the distance floated. My stomach turned and I only wondered how wonderful it would be to catch it. To my surprise it stopped. I looked around and I saw that the thread was stuck to the pumpkin tendril behind me. The joy I experienced was pure and even today it gives me goosebumps.

item.title: 4 PM
item.dc:creator: divyaprakashpoddar
item.content:encoded:
It has been quite a while and I have had enough rest, I thought to myself as I turned on my sides and tried to get a hold of my phone. It showed 4 O'clock in the evening. It indeed was time for me to end my siesta and get up. Lazily I put my foot down and proceeded towards the door leading to the bathroom to get fresh. I had a meeting to attend online and needed to make at least my face presentable.

I got to the door and held the doorknob but couldn't feel it. Things turned black and my eyes opened. I felt the warm bed underneath me. Turning around I saw the clock on the wall.

4 PM


What a strange dream, I thought to myself. But afternoon naps usually are responsible for such variants of dreams. My wife was sleeping next to me. I wondered if I should wake her up and tell her about it. I decided to let it go and get on with the routine to freshen up. I put my foot down and fell into an endless void.

I woke up with a sweaty forehead. The fall in the dream felt very real. Maybe I had made some noise in my dreams, as I could see my wife sitting next to me, trying to calm me down. I told her about the dream and she mocked me, thinking I was referring to the plot of the popular movie. I looked at the watch.

4 PM

In order to get some natural light to freshen up my senses, I pulled apart the curtains on the windows next to me. The sun was nearing the horizon, completing it's last leg of the day's journey. In a moment the light from sun went out and everything around me turned pitch black. After a moment's silence, the city erupted with roars of people from all around. My head started to hurt and I could feel darkness from the outside penetrating inside. I tried to shout but felt my consciousness fading away. The last thing I remembered was that I fell on my bed.

I got up but still couldn't see. I started panicking. It's all black now. I dare not open my eyes. I mean how long can this last? I'll probably be finally awake in a few hours. It's not like time runs very slowly in dreams. Right?? ?

wp:comment.wp:comment_content: you r not alone, I see too such real/future dreams.. : )

item.title: Spider-Man
item.dc:creator: divyaprakashpoddar
item.content:encoded:
Bill boards were a thing which fascinated me. After moving to Bangalore I would stop at every other bill board and marvel at its contents. I couldn't fathom how an artist could create such intricate artwork and such life like characters. (Something about flex printing). My favorite one was in Brigade road where the billboard displayed three images one after the other. The most awesome things of my entire year and I begged my parents to take me to brigade road just to see that spectacle and a comic store on the footpaths next to K C Das on church street. Among the many characters on the shiny comics one caught my eye since I could see it both on the book and on a billboard above the me. Spider-man it read! Coming Soon! just under it. My introduction to the character of spider-man was though a bill board.

I wondered what was so great about that character that a movie was being made about him. Flipping through the pages I soon realized it was a shameless rip-off our original comic Nagraj. The silly artists had and the people of Bangalore had put up movie posters in it's honor. Strange place I thought to myself.

However it had piqued my interest so I took that along with a Readers digest to get through my father's permission. It worked I had a shiny new comic with brilliant artwork to help me get through the weekend and the week/s beyond (It was in English after all). I was mostly interested in the artwork which I loved.

Going though the pages, spider-man seemed way more interesting than Nagraj and I even considered forgiving the authors for plagiarism. I was soon done with it. (Drawing pictures an'all)

Now it was time to get another one and thankfully a store had opened nearby our home in Ulsoor which was selling these comics. Brought up with Raj and Diamond Comics I was now moving into the world of Gotham comics.

<Insert Pic of your collection>

I went to the store the next day. While waiting for the store-keeper to get the comics for me from the upper shelves, I let my gaze wander up above to the sound of a passing airplane. The plane passed behind a bill-board into the webs of spider-man. He really was taking over the city.

What Rrra? (Never really understood the switch from Da to Ra) You havent heard of spider-man a?

No ..Ra/Da? I have not.

You can't miss the movie man! It's going to be epic!

I went home and swithced on the TV and one of the 12 channels was a channel provided by the cable operator on which The cable channel played Kaho Na Pyar Hai for the 20th time. I loved the movie and always wondered if a doppleganager lived somewhere in the foreign lands. But now the movie paused to show some advertisements of the local shops. I took out my comic and immeresed myself in it. I tried ignoring the drone of the boring monologue of the guy talking about his furniture store, however his drone was replaced by some action noises which made me look up. The man in my comics jumping about the screen and swinging across huge buildings in a city. He was spinning web from his hands, fighting an ugly green monster and kissing a beautiful girl upside down. I quickly changed the channel and had a look around. After confirming that the coast was clear, changed it back. Thankfully the trailer wasn't over. It ended with a screen saying it was coming to the theatres near us in Bangalore and I caught one of the names as Rex, Brigade Road. Now my favourite place had three amazing things, Picture changing bill-board, Comic book shop and Rex theatre. I couldn't wait for my father to come home and make my demands known to him.

The night (like most nights) was rainy. The auto dropped us right in front of the theatre.

The entire night I was swinging across the pubilc utility bulding and the tall citi bank towers.
